Impervious

im-PUR-vee-us -- stress on the second syllable, PUR. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impervious is impenetrable; unable to be passed through or affected.

The volcano's slopes are paved in rock impervious to water, so every rainstorm runs straight off into the sea.

Worked Example

A referee keeps a steady hand through ninety minutes of booing, players shouting in her face, and a coach hurling his clipboard -- then calls the final play exactly as she saw it.

She is impervious to the pressure: none of it gets through. Impervious began as a word for materials that water cannot penetrate and grew into a word for people that insults, criticism, or panic cannot penetrate either. Notice that it almost always brings the little word 'to' with it: impervious TO water, impervious TO pressure.

How Impervious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

impenetrable

impenetrable: impossible to pass through

impermeable

impermeable: not letting liquid pass through

unaffected

unaffected: not influenced or changed by something

Antonyms

permeable

permeable: allowing liquids or gases to pass through

susceptible

susceptible: easily affected or influenced

How Strong Is It? — unaffected → impervious → impenetrable

unaffected vs. impervious

unaffected vs. impervious: Unaffected is the milder, more everyday word -- an unaffected listener simply is not moved this time, while an impervious one could not be moved however long you kept trying.

impenetrable vs. impervious

impenetrable vs. impervious: Impenetrable presses impervious to its physical extreme: an impervious jacket keeps the rain out, while an impenetrable wall keeps out everything -- water, light, sound, and people alike.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of impervious.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before p) (Latin in-)

Root — per

Root — per: through (Latin per, 'through')

Root — vi

Root — vi: way, road (from Latin via, 'way, road'; its a drops before the ending)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: having; full of (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Im- ('not' -- in- always shifts to im- before p) + per ('through') + vi ('way', from Latin via; its a drops before the ending) + -ous spell impervious. Read the parts in order and the word means 'having no way through': water finds no way through an impervious roof; criticism finds no way through an impervious person.

Use the root in a new word: via

Use the root in a new word: via: We flew to Rome via Paris, changing planes in the middle of the night.

Root Check

Word Choice

Impervious nearly always takes the preposition 'to': impervious to water, impervious to heat, impervious to criticism, impervious to reason. If you write it without 'to,' the sentence will usually sound unfinished. The physical sense (nothing gets through the material) and the human sense (nothing gets through to the person) are equally common.
